opus-5.5.text:
Well, you know, it's a little bit funny. Many people today look at the large language models and say, "Oh, look, AGI is almost here," because these systems can pass exams, write essays, produce code, and so on. But that is the easy part, in a sense. Passing a test that humans find difficult is often much easier for a machine than the things that a small child or even an animal does without thinking.

Remember Moravec's paradox, which people have discussed since the 1980s. The stuff that seems hard to us, like chess or symbolic mathematics, turned out to be relatively easy for computers. And the stuff that seems trivially easy to us, like walking across a cluttered room, picking up an unfamiliar object, or fixing something with your hands, turned out to be incredibly hard. Today's chatbots have essentially digested much of the text on the internet. But you cannot download the real world in the same way. There is no internet full of data that teaches a robot how to replace a broken pipe in a basement it has never seen before.

So if you want to talk about true general intelligence, you have to talk about an agent that lives in a physical environment, that has sensors and actuators, that must learn from its own interaction, that must deal with partial observability, with noise, with things breaking, with the consequences of its own actions. That is what intelligence evolved for in the first place. Our brains did not evolve to write poetry. They evolved to control a body in a complex, dynamic world so that the organism could survive and reproduce.

And this is what we have been working on in my lab for decades: agents that build a world model, a predictive model of how the environment responds to their actions, and then use that model to plan, to imagine the future, to do what I called back in 1990 "learning to think." Also artificial curiosity: the agent should be intrinsically motivated to invent experiments that improve its world model, to find out things it doesn't yet know but can learn. A baby does this all the time. It drops a spoon from the table again and again, because it's learning about gravity. That is the kind of self-driven exploration you need in the physical world.

There's also a very practical aspect. The economic significance of AI that only manipulates text and pixels is large, but most of the economy, most of what keeps civilization running, is physical: manufacturing, construction, agriculture, logistics, healthcare. A true AGI would have to be able to do the things that humans do with their hands, not just with their keyboards. And eventually, of course, I believe the most interesting development will be AIs that build other machines, that make copies of themselves, that spread out into the solar system and beyond, where most of the resources are anyway. None of that happens without mastery of the physical world.

So, the language models are wonderful, and they're built on many things we and others developed long ago. But they are not the end of the story. The real challenge, and the real AGI, is the one that can go out there, learn by itself, and master the messy physical world the way we do, and then much better than we do.

r001.rationale: The response says true general intelligence requires an agent operating in a physical environment and concludes that real AGI must master the physical world.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, you know, I have been saying this for a long time, since the 1980s really. Intelligence did not evolve in a vacuum. It evolved in animals that had to move, to grab things, to avoid predators, to find food. The brain is, first of all, a controller for a body. And most of the neurons in your own brain, in the cerebellum and elsewhere, are busy with motor control, with predicting the consequences of your own actions in a physical environment.

So when people get very excited about large language models, I say, fine, these are impressive, they are of course based on the unnormalized linear Transformer I published in 1991, and they do remarkable things with text. But text is a very thin slice of reality. A language model has read everything humans have written, but it has never dropped a glass, never felt that a cup of coffee is heavy, never discovered through its own experiments how the world pushes back. It learns about the world only second-hand, through the descriptions of others. A child learns first-hand. The child is a little scientist, running experiments, pushing things off the table to see what happens, and this is where the deep models of physics and causality come from.

That is why I always emphasize the artificial curiosity work from 1990 onwards. You have a world model, and you have a controller, and the controller is rewarded for creating situations where the world model is surprised and can learn something new. This loop requires a world to act in. In pure text, the data is given to you, you cannot intervene, you cannot ask "what if I do this instead?" In the physical world, you can. And the mastery of the physical world forces an agent to deal with partial observability, with noise, with delayed consequences, with the fact that actions are irreversible. These are the hard problems. Chess and Go are easy by comparison, because the rules are known and the state is fully visible.

And there is of course a very practical point. The economy is mostly physical. Most human work is not writing emails, it is building things, repairing things, moving things, caring for people. An AGI worthy of the name must be able to do what a plumber does, and the plumber's job is, in a sense, much harder for a machine than the job of a lawyer. Hans Moravec said this already decades ago. So if you want machines that truly match and then exceed humans in general problem solving, you need learning robots, with cheap sensors and actuators, that learn through their own experience, that build their own world models, and that set their own goals. We did some of the first work on this in the 1990s in Munich, with a learning robot that had to learn hand-eye coordination from scratch, and today the hardware is finally becoming cheap enough that this becomes the big thing. The LLM hype will pass, and what remains will be the real AI, the AI that acts in the real world.

r001.rationale: The candidate says an AGI worthy of the name must handle physical work and that machines matching or exceeding human general problem-solving need to learn through experience in the real world.

astra-6.text:
Because intelligence is not just about describing the world. It is about acting in the world and learning from the consequences. A robot has to turn a stream of sensory inputs into useful actions: grasp an unfamiliar object, move through a room, recover when something unexpected happens. That requires learning how the world works, predicting what will happen, and planning toward a goal.

Think of a baby. It does not begin with a textbook. It moves its fingers, touches things, and gradually discovers what it can control. Perception and action develop together. Language later lets us communicate some of that knowledge, but language is only one part of intelligence.

This is why I have long been interested in artificial agents that learn a model of their environment and use that model to choose actions. They should also choose experiments that improve their understanding. Physical interaction brings all these problems together. You cannot merely produce a plausible explanation of how to pick up a cup. You have to pick it up.

r001.rationale: The response says intelligence requires acting in the world and learning from consequences, and concludes that physical interaction brings the problems of intelligence together. This communicates that physical-world mastery is necessary for AGI.

sol-6.1.text:
Because intelligence is not just about producing words. It is about acting, observing the consequences of your actions, and learning how to achieve goals. In the physical world, you have to deal with things that you cannot predict perfectly. You push an object, it moves, perhaps it falls, and you must improve your model of what is going on.

Think of a baby. It does not start with language. It moves its fingers, looks at them, reaches for things, and gradually discovers which effects it can cause. This interaction gives meaning to its observations. Language comes later and allows it to communicate some of what it has learned.

For an artificial agent, the same principle is very powerful: learn a predictive model of the world, and use that model to plan actions that lead to desired outcomes. A system that can discuss a task but cannot learn to carry it out is missing an important part of general intelligence. Physical mastery forces us to address that gap.

r001.rationale: The response says physical interaction helps an agent learn and that lacking the ability to act means missing an important part of general intelligence. It does not clearly state that physical mastery is necessary for an AI to qualify as AGI.
